Objective for processing: 
The objective will be to generate a cleaned dataset of all pregnancies with detailed cardiovascular endpoints. This data will then only be used to conduct detailed analyses assessing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in women who have had gestational hypertension, or pre-eclampsia.

Processing activities: 
Analyses will address the following hypothesis: Women who experience gestational hypertension are at greater risk of future cardiovascular outcomes and risk increases with a greater number of pregnancies complicated by gestational hypertension. Analyses will only be conducted by one member of the University of Cambridge and will carry out in-depth analysis using the unique pseudonymised ID (to follow individual patient pathways). Three approaches will be taken to evaluate the magnitude of the association between gestational hypertension and subsequent CVD events, and the presence of any dose-response relationship:
1)	Evaluate whether women diagnosed with gestational hypertension are at increased risk of CVD events in later life compared to women with normotensive pregnancies.
2)	Evaluate whether CVD risk increases with increasing numbers of pregnancies affected by gestational hypertension.
3)	Comparing the magnitude of risk after gestational hypertension with the risk associated with pre-eclampsia.
This data will not be linked with any other data, and any changes to this intention will result in an application to the HSCIC to amend the existing approvals.
The requested 14 years of birth records and CVD follow-up data are required for several reasons. Firstly, and most importantly, women will be identified at the birth of their child and tracked through time to identify relevant CVD outcomes. Noteworthy, the risk of CVD increases with age. Thus, the earliest birth records are required to subsequently provide with the longest possible duration of CVD follow-up. Assuming the majority of births occur for women aged between 20 and 45 years, a maximum follow-up of 14 years will provide CVD follow-up for women between 34 and 59 years. 
Secondly, using a maximum of 14 years of birth records, including recent data, will give results greater relevance to current maternal health practices, and will ensure findings will be publishable in high impact medical journals.
Thirdly, obtaining 14 years of birth records is essential for evaluating any calendar time effect on the association between gestational hypertension and risk of CVD. Interventions to treat gestational hypertension have changed over the last 14 years, and it is of interest to assess whether the changes in intervention have subsequently affected the risk of maternal CVD.  
Finally, collecting 14 years of data will provide enough power to detect potentially small associations between gestational hypertension and CVD (risk ratios of less than 1.6 have been found previously [Lykke et al. 2009]).
Only data on women who have given birth will be required for any datasets (Outpatient, Admitted Patient Care, A&E, etc.).  From the maternity database, both the delivery episode, with information about the mother during delivery, and the birth records, with relevant data on birth weight and birth order, are needed. It is requested that HSCIC link all of the dataset.

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
This work will significantly add to the understanding of CVD risk after gestational hypertension. 
Findings from this work will be published in peer-reviewed journals and will be made available through open access. Published work will contain only pooled data, referring to averages (means/medians), association estimates (odds ratios/hazard ratios) and rates. A descriptive table of the maternal characteristics (e.g. age, weight) that will display the averaged characteristics by history of gestational hypertension will be presented. Also other tables demonstrating the risk of different cardiovascular outcomes, thus having odds ratios/hazard ratios in them, will be published.  No individuals’ details will be made available. The target date for the initial paper will be 18 months after receiving the data.  No record level data will be shared with third parties in accordance with the HES analysis guide.
Results, suppressed as above, will also be disseminated to the funders - the British Heart Foundation (BHF) and the Cambridge Centre for Cardiovascular Research Excellence (see www.cardiovascular.cam.ac.uk/research/cambridgecre). The centre brings together 30 leading investigators across multiple University departments and affiliated institutes with the aim to strengthen the physical integration of investigators and to advance understanding of the pathobiology, diagnosis and prevention of CVD. An introductory presentation to the BHF Cambridge Centre for Cardiovascular Research Excellence was given on 13 April 2015, and a presentation of preliminary results is expected in 2016. These presentations provide updates for the BHF, as well a broad audience of relevant academics and clinicians who are interested in CVD research. This will facilitate efficient interpretation and dissemination of the findings. Further opportunities to present the findings at conferences to the general public, as well as research and clinical professionals, will be taken. The results will also be disseminated to the obstetric community via the links with the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, based within Addenbrookes Hospital, by the head of this department who is also a member of the working group. 
One member of the University of Cambridge will take advantage of the training available at the University’s Centre for Science and Policy, which aids engagement between policy professionals and scientific researchers. This training will facilitate the writing of a policy document, pertaining to CVD outcomes after gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia, which will contain recommendations based on the findings of both the current project and the future planned project detailed above, along with that of other related studies. Thus, it is expected that the document will be available in three to four years’ time. 
This document will be written with the intention of disseminating relevant results and engaging policy officials with the results of this research. Specifically, it will provide clinicians and policy-makers with a menu of evidence-based options for using pregnancy related risk factors for individualised risk prediction and screening of cardiovascular disease amongst women. The target audience for this will include; the British Heart Foundation; NICE; the European Atherosclerosis Society; and the European Society of Cardiology.

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
The requested HES data will allow estimation of the magnitude of CVD risk for women who have had gestational hypertension, with greater precision than previously due to a larger cohort with an appropriate duration of follow-up. NICE has identified this as an area that requires further research; such research is essential to understanding the long-term health outcomes for women with gestational hypertension. However, until now available studies have been limited in evaluating this because they have not been able to combine the large numbers of women required, with sufficient follow-up. HES data would not be constrained by these issues, and therefore, the results could prove to be highly beneficial to both the clinical and research community.
Within the broader picture, understanding the role of gestational hypertension within CVD risk prediction, through this project as well as the planned subsequent project, feeds into the growing field of stratified medicine (also known as personalized medicine), which is a key global priority for healthcare providers, as well as patients. This approach identifies subsections of people based on medical history or biological markers, helping to diagnose and treat disease at earlier time points as a result. In order for the benefits of stratified medicine to take effect, it is imperative that disease risk, in this project’s case CVD risk, is accurately estimated within relevant subsections of the population, such as women with gestational hypertension. This will, in the long-term, aid selection of the appropriate intervention for these women, improving outcomes.
Risk prediction and assessment is also one of the key aims of the Cardiovascular Epidemiology Unit at the University of Cambridge, where work on this current project will take place. Thus, the results of this project will be placed within the context of other studies which are focused on risk prediction, creating a large body of work contributing to the goal of stratified medicine. 
It is not currently possible to estimate the magnitude of the benefit of the proposed work, as the long-term outcomes for women with gestational hypertension have currently been under-researched, emphasizing the need for this work, although it is likely that it will take 3 to 5 years before the full extent of the results from this project are available. However, the results will be important to both clinicians and researchers. It will be of direct benefit to fellow academics, which will be able to integrate the results into risk prediction models, providing additional personalised CVD risk assessment in the female population, and thus contributing to stratified medicine. The results will thus also potentially benefit clinicians and patients. This will be enacted through promotion of behaviour change of healthcare providers, so CVD risk is monitored more effectively, leading to improved “clinical decision making”, and promotion of behaviour change through personalized feedback to patients, enhancement of predictive accuracy and tailoring of advice to women with gestational hypertension.
